overview:
On the western edge of the Balkan Peninsula, Albania faces Italy across the Adriatic and Ionian Seas. It is a small country, about the size of the US state of Maryland, but it packs in snowy mountains, wild rivers, olive groves, and a long coastline of turquoise bays known as the Albanian Riviera. The capital, Tirana, is famous for apartment blocks painted in bold oranges, purples, and greens, an idea launched by a mayor who was also a painter.

About 2.8 million people live in Albania, and millions more Albanians live in neighboring Kosovo, North Macedonia, Italy, and beyond. The language, Albanian, forms its own separate branch of the Indo-European family, related to no other living tongue. For most of the 20th century the country was cut off from the world under a strict communist government, but since the early 1990s it has become a parliamentary republic, joined NATO, and applied to join the European Union. Tourism is growing fast as visitors discover its beaches and mountain villages.
landAndNature: Roughly seven-tenths of Albania is mountainous. In the far north rise the Albanian Alps, nicknamed the Accursed Mountains for their jagged, hard-to-cross peaks, where shepherds still move flocks to high pastures each summer. The Vjosa River flows for about 270 kilometers without a single dam, which earned it protection in 2023 as Europe's first wild-river national park. Lake Ohrid, shared with North Macedonia, is more than a million years old and home to fish found nowhere else. The coast has a warm Mediterranean climate, while inland winters bring deep snow. Brown bears, wolves, and the extremely rare Balkan lynx survive in the forests, and Dalmatian pelicans nest in the Karavasta Lagoon.
peopleAndCulture: Albanians speak two main dialects, Gheg in the north and Tosk in the south. Most people are Muslim, with large Orthodox and Catholic Christian communities, and the country is known for religious tolerance. Hospitality is a point of honor: an old code called besa means keeping a promise and protecting guests at any cost. Meals often begin with byrek, a flaky pastry filled with cheese or spinach, and might include tavë kosi, lamb baked with yogurt. In the south, groups sing iso-polyphony, a layered style of harmony recognized by UNESCO. Soccer is the favorite sport, and strong coffee served slowly in cafés is a daily ritual. Mother Teresa, the famous nun, was ethnically Albanian.
history: The Illyrians lived here more than 2,000 years ago, followed by Roman and Byzantine rule. In the 1400s the national hero Gjergj Kastrioti, known as Skanderbeg, held off the Ottoman Empire for 25 years, but Albania eventually spent more than four centuries under Ottoman control. Independence was declared in 1912. After World War II, communist leader Enver Hoxha ruled from 1944 until his death in 1985. He banned religion, sealed the borders, and had roughly 170,000 concrete bunkers built in case of invasion. Communism collapsed in 1991, and hard years of poverty and emigration followed. Albania joined NATO in 2009 and has been a candidate to join the European Union since 2014.
funFacts: Albanians call their country Shqipëri, often translated as Land of the Eagles, which explains the black double-headed eagle on the red flag.
Some of the country's 170,000 Cold War bunkers have been turned into museums, cafés, and even a hostel.
In Albania, a sideways shake of the head traditionally means yes, and a nod means no, the opposite of most of Europe.
Lake Ohrid is one of the oldest lakes on Earth and holds about 200 species that live nowhere else.
The ancient city of Butrint has ruins from Greek, Roman, Byzantine, and Venetian times layered on one small peninsula.
